title: Federated Domain Generalization for Time-Series Classification via Dynamics-to-Domain Generation

problem.claim: Federated time-series classification must handle non-stationary, heterogeneous sensor streams and out-of-distribution shifts when clients have small, biased data subsets.

gap.claim: Limited client diversity makes it difficult to learn robust invariances for federated domain generalization.

contributions.claim: FedD2G is a dynamics-aware generative framework for federated domain generalization.
FedD2G decomposes sequences into segments and learns dual-view dynamic descriptors from time-domain morphology and frequency-domain periodic cues.
Sequence-Fused Transition sampling uses a class-conditioned Markov transition model to synthesize temporally coherent sequences without sharing raw signals.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on cross-domain federated time-series benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong federated learning and federated domain generalization baselines, reaching 78.5% average accuracy under small-scale data availability.
The authors report empirical evidence that learned dynamics reveal latent domain variants and guide source-target gap reduction through distributional expansion.

narrative_sequence.summary: Time-series classification faces distribution shifts from non-stationary and heterogeneous sensor streams, especially in federated settings.
Small and biased client datasets provide insufficient diversity for learning robust invariances.
The approach interprets domain shift through fine-grained local behaviors and temporal transitions represented by latent segment dynamics.
FedD2G learns dual-view segment dynamics and uses transition-based sampling to generate temporally coherent sequences beyond observed source distributions without sharing raw signals.
The authors report benchmark improvements and evidence that learned dynamics expose latent domain variants and help bridge source-target gaps.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify dataset identities, client counts, data partitions, baseline configurations, or statistical uncertainty.
